title: Non-standard evaluation in R

When we write `select(penguins, species)`,
`species` is not an object in our environment,
yet the code works.
Normally, R evaluates every argument we give a function:
it looks up `species`, and stops with an error if it cannot find it.
Functions like `select()` instead capture the code we typed
and evaluate it somewhere else, such as inside a data frame.
This is called **non-standard evaluation** (NSE).
The `tidyverse` way of doing it is called **tidy evaluation**,
and it is built on three ideas:

1. **Quoting and unquoting:**
   capturing code without running it,
   and inserting values into captured code.
2. **Quosures:**
   captured code together with the environment it was written in.
3. **The data mask:**
   evaluating code so that the columns of a data frame are found before other objects.

This chapter builds up these ideas by writing our own simple version of `select()`, step by step.
It is adapted from the talk
[Learning Tidy Evaluation by Reimplementing `dplyr`](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WoBbQ5gsbgU)
by Daniel Chen
([slides and code](https://github.com/chendaniely/rstatsdc-2020-tidyeval)),
updated for the current versions of the `tidyverse`.
If you are looking for which pattern to use in your own code,
rather than how it works,
see the "Programming with the `tidyverse` functions" section of the
[Defining functions in R](9020-functions-r.qmd) appendix (@sec-tidyverse-patterns).

We use the `rlang` package, which implements tidy evaluation,
and the `penguins` data set from the `palmerpenguins` package:

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(rlang)
library(palmerpenguins)

penguins
```

## Many ways to select columns

R has many ways of selecting columns from a data frame.
Most of them take the column name as a string, or the column's position:

```{r}
penguins[, c("species", "island")]
```

```{r}
penguins[, c(1, 3, 5)]
```

```{r}
#| results: hide
penguins$species
penguins[["species"]]
```

Two of them take the bare column name, without quotes:

```{r}
subset(penguins, select = species)
```

```{r}
select(penguins, species)
```

So non-standard evaluation is not just a `tidyverse` thing:
base R's `subset()` uses it too.
But if we try to use a bare column name with `[`,
R evaluates `species` as an object in our environment,
and there is no such object:

```{r}
penguins[, species]
```

## Quoting code: expressions

When we type `3 + 3`, R evaluates it straight away:

```{r}
3 + 3
```

`quote()` captures the code instead of running it.
The result is called an **expression**:

```{r}
ex <- quote(3 + 3)
ex
```

We can run the expression later with `eval()`:

```{r}
eval(ex)
```

`rlang::expr()` does the same thing as `quote()`:

```{r}
expr(3 + 3)
```

You can think of an expression as the code before it runs.
It is not a string, but that is a reasonable first approximation.
A bare name like `species` is a special kind of expression, called a **symbol**,
and `3 + 3`, which calls the function `+`, is called a **call**:

```{r}
str(quote(species))
```

```{r}
str(quote(3 + 3))
```

The `rlang` documentation calls quoting **defusing**:
the code is captured like a defused bomb, so that it does not go off until we decide.

## Rebuilding `select()`

### Try 1: strings

Our first `my_select()` passes the column name straight to `[`:

```{r}
my_select <- function(data, col) {
  data[, col, drop = FALSE]
}
```

It works when we give it a string:

```{r}
my_select(penguins, "species")
```

but not with a bare column name,
because R evaluates `species` as soon as `[` needs the value of `col`:

```{r}
my_select(penguins, species)
```

So we need to quote what the user typed, instead of evaluating it.

### Try 2: quoting inside the function

`expr()` quotes exactly what we type, so inside a function,
`expr(col)` gives us the symbol `col`: the name of the argument,
not what the user passed to it:

```{r}
f_expr <- function(x) {
  expr(x)
}

f_expr(hello)
```

To capture what the user typed,
we need the "enriched" version, `enexpr()`:

```{r}
f_enexpr <- function(x) {
  enexpr(x)
}

f_enexpr(hello)
```

The `en` prefix means "capture the code given to this argument".

### Try 3: capturing what the user typed

Now we can capture the user's column names with `enexprs()`
(the plural of `enexpr()`, for `...`),
turn them into strings,
find their positions with `match()`,
and subset the data on those positions with regular base R:

```{r}
my_select <- function(data, ...) {
  cols <- enexprs(...)                             # quote what the user typed
  cols_chr <- as.vector(cols, mode = "character")  # turn the expressions into strings
  idx <- match(cols_chr, names(data))              # find the column positions
  data[, idx, drop = FALSE]                        # regular base R
}
```

```{r}
my_select(penguins, species, year, "island")
```

It works on a `data.frame` as well as a tibble:

```{r}
head(my_select(iris, Species, Petal.Width))
```

This is the general idea behind `select()`:
work out the positions of the columns the user asked for,
then subset the data on those positions.

## Unquoting: `!!` and `!!!`

What if the column name is stored in a variable?

```{r}
col_name <- "species"
my_select(penguins, col_name, island)
```

Our function quoted `col_name` as the symbol `col_name`,
and there is no column with that name.
We need a way to tell a quoting function
"use the *value* of this variable, not its name".
That is what `!!` (pronounced "bang-bang") does:
it **unquotes** (`rlang` calls it **injects**) a value into the code before the function captures it:

```{r}
my_select(penguins, !!col_name, island)
```

`!!!` ("bang-bang-bang") does the same for a list of values,
inserting each one as a separate argument
(similar to `*args` in Python).
`rlang` calls this **splicing**:

```{r}
cols <- exprs(species, island, year)
my_select(penguins, !!!cols)
```

`!!` and `!!!` only work inside functions that quote their arguments
with `enexpr()`, `enquo()`, `{{ }}` and friends (and in `rlang::inject()`).
Anywhere else, `!!` is just two `!` (not) operators in a row:

```{r}
!!TRUE
```

## Quosures: code plus its environment

### Environments

An expression on its own does not say where to find the objects it uses.
`eval()` looks them up in an **environment**:
a collection of named objects, like the global environment you work in.

```{r}
e <- new.env()
e$z <- 3

eval(quote(3 + z))
```

```{r}
eval(quote(3 + z), envir = e)
```

### Quosures

A **quosure** (quote + closure) is an expression bundled with the environment it was created in,
so it always knows where to look up its objects.
`enquo()` and `enquos()` capture arguments as quosures
(`quo()` and `new_quosure()` also exist, but you rarely need them).
`rlang::eval_tidy()` evaluates a quosure in its own environment:

```{r}
q <- new_quosure(expr(3 + z), env = e)
q
```

```{r}
eval_tidy(q)
```

Why does this matter?
The code a user passes to your function should be evaluated where the user wrote it,
so that it finds *their* objects, not the objects inside your function.
Here, both functions create their own `x`,
but only the quosure version uses the user's `x`:

```{r}
x <- 100

times_two_expr <- function(arg) {
  x <- 1
  eval(enexpr(arg))
}

times_two_quo <- function(arg) {
  x <- 1
  eval_tidy(enquo(arg))
}
```

```{r}
times_two_expr(x * 2)
```

```{r}
times_two_quo(x * 2)
```

Formulas (`~`) work the same way:
a formula is an expression plus the environment it was created in,
which is why model formulas can find the variables you use in them.

## The data mask

`eval_tidy()` can also take a data frame (or a list) as its `data` argument.
The columns of the data are then found *before* the objects in the quosure's environment.
This is the **data mask**: the data "masks" the environment.

```{r}
q1 <- new_quosure(expr(x * y), env(x = 100))
df <- data.frame(y = 1:5)

eval_tidy(q1, data = df)
```

`y` was found in the data, and `x` in the quosure's environment.
This is how `filter(penguins, species == "Gentoo")` finds the `species` column.

### Try 4: quosures and a data mask

Now we can make `my_select()` work like `select()` does:
we evaluate each argument in a data mask where every column name stands for its position.
A bare column name evaluates to its position,
a number stays a number,
and anything else (like a variable holding a string)
is evaluated in the user's environment:

```{r}
my_select <- function(data, ...) {
  cols <- enquos(...)                                      # quote what the user typed
  positions <- as.list(set_names(seq_along(data), names(data))) # column name = position
  idx <- vapply(cols, function(col) {
    value <- eval_tidy(col, data = positions)              # evaluate in the data mask
    as.integer(if (is.character(value)) positions[[value]] else value)
  }, integer(1))
  data[, idx, drop = FALSE]                                # regular base R
}
```

```{r}
col_name <- "species"
my_select(penguins, col_name, year, "island", 6)
```

`col_name` is not a column,
so it is found in our environment, where it holds `"species"`,
without needing `!!`.

### Collisions: the data mask ambiguity

What if the data *does* have a column called `col_name`?

```{r}
penguins_extra <- mutate(penguins, col_name = 0)

my_select(penguins_extra, col_name, island)
```

The column wins, and we get the wrong column, with no error.
This is called the [data mask ambiguity](https://rlang.r-lib.org/reference/topic-data-mask-ambiguity.html):
when a column and an object in our environment have the same name,
the data mask picks the column.

This is exactly the quirk of `pull(all_of(col))` described in @sec-tidyverse-pull.
`pull()` is built on `tidyselect::vars_pull()`,
which evaluates its argument in a data mask of column positions,
just like our `my_select()`:

```{r}
body(tidyselect::vars_pull)
```

So inside `pull(all_of(col))`,
`col` is looked up in the data first,
and if the data has a column called `col`,
`all_of()` receives that column's position instead of our string.

### The `.data` and `.env` pronouns

To remove the ambiguity, `eval_tidy()` provides two **pronouns** in every data mask:
`.data`, which only looks in the data,
and `.env`, which only looks in the environment.
They work in our `my_select()` too:

```{r}
my_select(penguins_extra, .env$col_name, island)
```

and in every `tidyverse` function that uses data masking:

```{r}
df <- data.frame(x = NA, y = 2)
x <- 100

mutate(df, y = y / x)
```

```{r}
mutate(df, y = y / .env$x)
```

`.data[[var]]` evaluates `var` in the environment,
and then looks up the column with that name only in the data,
so it cannot collide with a column called `var`.
That is why `.data[[col]]` is the safe way to use a column name stored in a string,
including in `pull()`.

## Back to the `tidyverse`

With these pieces, the patterns from the
[Defining functions in R](9020-functions-r.qmd) appendix are less mysterious.

`{{ col }}` is shorthand for capturing an argument as a quosure and injecting it:
`!!enquo(col)`.
These two functions are the same:

```{r}
filter_penguins <- function(col, val) {
  col <- enquo(col)
  filter(penguins, !!col == val)
}

filter_penguins(species, "Chinstrap")
```

```{r}
filter_penguins <- function(col, val) {
  filter(penguins, {{ col }} == val)
}

filter_penguins(species, "Chinstrap")
```

`.data[[col]]` uses the `.data` pronoun from the data mask,
and `all_of(cols)` is how tidy selection takes a vector of names from the environment.

The talk this chapter is based on ended with a table of four cases:
does the user pass a string or a bare name,
and does the function you are calling need a string or a bare name?
Here they are with today's recommended tools:

| The user passes | The function needs | Use                                                                 |
|-----------------|--------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------|
| a string        | a string           | the string, as is: `penguins[[col]]`                                |
| a string        | a bare name        | `.data[[col]]` in data masking, `all_of(col)` in tidy selection     |
| a bare name     | a string           | `as_name(enquo(col))`, or `englue("{{ col }}")` to build a longer string |
| a bare name     | a bare name        | `{{ col }}`                                                         |

For example, a bare name can be turned into a string for a title or a file name:

```{r}
mean_label <- function(col) {
  englue("Mean of {{ col }}")
}

mean_label(body_mass_g)
```

Some patterns from 2020 are no longer recommended:

- `aes_string()` in `ggplot2` is deprecated (since `ggplot2` 3.0.0).
  Use `aes(x = .data[[col]])` for strings and `aes(x = {{ col }})` for bare names.
- Turning a string into code with `rlang::parse_expr()` and then injecting it with `!!`
  runs whatever the string contains as code,
  and fails on column names that are not valid R names:

  ```{r}
  parse_expr("body mass")
  ```

  Use `.data[[col]]` instead, which treats the string as a name and nothing else.
